ramayana-homecoming-6-130-21.plain: At the coronation, Rama gives his beloved queen Sita a shining pearl necklace. She wears it for a moment, then takes it off, looks at the Vanars (the monkey warriors who helped rescue her), and looks at Rama as if silently asking him something.
themes: wanting to thank those who helped

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-22.plain: Rama understands Sita's silent question. He tells her to give the necklace to the one who is wise, truthful and strong, the loyal friend who stayed with them through every danger to the end.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-23.plain: Sita places the necklace around Hanuman's neck, the monkey hero who found her in Lanka. It shines on him like moonlight on a hill.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-24.plain: Rama gives rich gifts to every Vanar, and they go home happy. For ten thousand years Ayodhya (Rama's kingdom) lived in peace under his rule, with no wives widowed by violence and no homes left empty.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-25.plain: Under Rama's rule, animals were free of disease and herds grew. The land gave plenty of food, no harvest failed, and no children died. There was no poverty, sickness or crime, and life was calm and happy.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-10.plain: Jatayu, the dying old vulture, points out the proof of his fight with Ravana, the demon king: the broken bow, the arrows, the smashed chariot, and the driver he struck down with his wings.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-11.plain: Jatayu explains that he grew tired because he was old, and Ravana cut off his wings with a sword and flew away with Sita through the sky. He asks Rama not to attack him, since he is already dying from Ravana's blow.
themes: fighting even when you might lose

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-12.plain: When Rama hears how bravely Jatayu fought for Sita, he puts down his bow and hugs the bird gently. Then Rama falls to the ground, and both brothers cry, because Rama feels two sorrows at once: losing Sita and seeing his friend dying.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-13.plain: Rama looks at the lonely, gasping bird in the forest, and as his sorrow rises again, he speaks to his brother Lakshmana.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-14.plain: Rama says he has lost his kingdom, his wife is gone, and now the bird is dying. He feels so unlucky that even the ocean would dry up if he tried to cool off in it.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-15.plain: Rama says no one in the world is as unlucky as he is, caught in a net of misery. Even Jatayu, the best of birds and a friend loved by his father King Dasharatha, now lies dying because of Rama's troubles.
themes: guilt when others suffer for you

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-16.plain: Rama and Lakshmana mourn the bird with pity and stroke his body as if he were their own father. Rama holds the blood-covered bird close to his chest.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-17.plain: Rama falls down crying many tears and calls out, asking where his beloved wife Sita, dearer to him than life, has gone.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-1.plain: Looking at the vulture killed by the demon, Rama feels deep pain and speaks lovingly to his brother Lakshmana.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-2.plain: Rama tells Lakshmana that this loyal bird fought for him and is giving his life for him. He points out the bleeding wounds and says the bird will soon die.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-3.plain: Rama sees Jatayu is too weak to speak or lift his eyes. He begs him, if he still can, to tell what happened to Sita and how he was hurt.
themes: searching for a lost loved one

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-4.plain: Rama asks why Ravana stole his wife and what wrong Rama did to deserve it. He also asks how Sita looked and what she said.
themes: wanting to know they were okay

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-5.plain: Rama asks Jatayu to tell him about Ravana's strength, his deeds, what form he takes, and where he lives.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-6.plain: Jatayu looks at the grieving Rama and, in a weak voice, says that Ravana, king of the demons, stole Sita from Rama's home.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-7.plain: Jatayu says Ravana used magic to create wind, clouds and darkness. When Jatayu grew tired, Ravana cut his wings, grabbed Sita, and flew south.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-8.plain: Jatayu says he is gasping and his eyesight is fading; he sees visions of golden trees as he dies. But he says the time Ravana chose for his crime will bring Ravana great trouble.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-9.plain: Jatayu explains that Ravana stole Sita at a special hour called Vinda, when anything stolen is always recovered by its owner. Like a fish that bites the bait, Ravana will soon meet his end.
themes: hope of getting back what was lost

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-10.plain: Jatayu tells Rama to calm his heart and stop grieving, because Rama will kill Ravana in battle and be happy with Sita again.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-11.plain: Still clear in mind despite his pain, Jatayu says Ravana is the son of the sage Vishravas and brother of Kubera, the Lord of Wealth. Then, bleeding, he takes his last breath.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-12.plain: Rama joins his palms in respect and begs Jatayu to speak again, but the bird's spirit has already left for heaven, and his body lies still on the ground.
themes: grief at the moment of death

ramayana-shabari-3-75-11.plain: After Shabari, an old forest devotee, offers Rama her stored fruits, Rama answers her kindly. He says Danu, a spirit he met earlier, told him about the great power of her teachers, and he would like to see their holy places for himself.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-12.plain: Shabari stands up and leads Rama and his brother Lakshmana through the forest around her home. She shows them the grove of Matanga, her teacher, which is famous everywhere.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-13.plain: Shabari describes the dark, thick forest full of deer and happy birds. She shows them the altar where her old teachers, with shaking hands, offered flowers every day while she served them.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-14.plain: Shabari says the holy power the sages earned through their self-discipline still makes their altar glow with light. She points to seven lakes that the sages, too weak from age and fasting to walk to them, pulled close by the power of their minds.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-15.plain: Shabari shows Rama the bark clothes the sages hung on trees after bathing, which are still wet after many days. The flowers they used in worship have also stayed fresh and never faded, because of the sages' power.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-16.plain: Having shown Rama everything, Shabari asks his permission to leave her body. She wants to go and live with the great sages she served so faithfully in this forest.
themes: longing for loved ones who passed

ramayana-shabari-3-75-17.plain: Rama and Lakshmana are amazed and filled with joy at Shabari's request, and they praise her. Rama tells her, "Go, lady, wherever you wish, for you have honored me well."

ramayana-shabari-3-75-19.plain: Through deep meditation, Shabari reached the holy heavenly world where pure-hearted sages live in joy that never ends.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-1.plain: Hanuman, son of the Wind-God and a messenger for the monkey king Sugriva, goes down from Rishyamuka mountain to meet Rama and Lakshmana. To be careful, he hides his monkey form and disguises himself as a wandering beggar-monk.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-2.plain: Hanuman bows at the brothers' feet with respect. Then he speaks to them truthfully and politely, praising them.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-3.plain: Hanuman greets them as holy young hermits who shine like gods or saintly kings. He asks how they came to this place by the Pampa lake, scaring the deer as they search among the trees.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-4.plain: Hanuman says their faces make the river look even more beautiful. He asks who they are, dressed in hermit's bark clothes, and notes that they sigh often as if in sorrow.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-5.plain: Hanuman praises the brothers as strong and brave, walking like lions and bulls. Each holds a bow like that of Indra, king of the gods.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-6.plain: Hanuman compares their arms to elephants' trunks and says the mountain glows with their presence. He asks how such god-like princes, with lotus-like eyes, came to this lonely place dressed with hermit's coiled hair.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-7.plain: Hanuman says they look like gods who came down from heaven, like the sun and moon visiting earth. He praises their broad chests, lion-like shoulders and strong, long arms.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-8.plain: Hanuman asks why they wear no jewels, though they look born to wear them. He says each of them seems fit to rule the whole earth, from Mount Meru to the Vindhya mountains.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-9.plain: Hanuman admires their gold-decorated bows, which shine like Indra's weapons. Their golden quivers are full of sharp arrows that look like fiery snakes.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-10.plain: Hanuman says their gold-inlaid swords flash like snakes that have shed their old skin. Then he asks why they stay silent and do not answer his questions.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-11.plain: Hanuman now reveals himself. He says Sugriva, the good king of the vanaras (monkey people), has been driven from his kingdom and wanders sadly. Sugriva has sent Hanuman because he wants to become their friend and ally.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-12.plain: Hanuman says he is one of Sugriva's chief helpers and the son of the Wind-God. He can travel anywhere freely, and he came from Rishyamuka hill dressed as a beggar to help his king's hopes.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-1.plain: Bharat, Rama's younger brother who ruled while Rama was in exile, folds his hands and gives the kingdom back. He says it is unharmed, but carrying the job was very hard for him.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-2.plain: Bharat says the burden nearly broke him, like a young ox not used to the yoke. He compares himself to a crow or a mule next to Rama, who is like a swan or a fast horse, and says he cannot walk the hard road a king must walk.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-3.plain: Bharat begs Rama to start ruling as everyone wants. He asks for the old ceremony of crowning, where holy water is poured on the new king's head.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-4.plain: Rama nods to agree. Barbers cut his long, tangled hair from his years in the forest, and after bathing he puts on royal clothes and looks splendid.
themes: getting ready for a new role

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-5.plain: Sita, Rama's wife, is dressed in shining robes with the help of older women. Sumantra, the royal charioteer, brings the chariot to the forest retreat on Shatrughna's order.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-6.plain: Sita and the wives of Sugriva, the monkey king, climb into the chariot, eager to see the city of Ayodhya. The chariot speeds off, as grand as the god Indra riding through the sky.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-7.plain: Rama rides home shining with glory. His brothers serve him: Bharat drives, Shatrughna holds the white royal umbrella over him, and Lakshmana fans him with a chourie, a royal fan made of a yak's tail.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-8.plain: Vibhishana, the new king of Lanka, helps Lakshmana fan Rama. Sugriva rides a huge elephant, and thousands of monkey (Vanara) chiefs follow in human form, dressed in rich clothes and jewels.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-9.plain: Rama reaches the gate of Ayodhya with conch shells, drums and shouts of "He comes!" Priests and cows lead the parade, and young women throw grain and gold.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-10.plain: Under rows of flags and among singing crowds, Rama nears the palace. He speaks to Bharat, the most dutiful of brothers, and tells him to go ahead into the king's hall.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-11.plain: Rama asks Bharat to take the monkey chiefs to greet their father's widows, the queen mothers. He also asks that Sugriva be given the very best rooms, decorated with gems, with lovely gardens.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-12.plain: Bharat agrees and leads Sugriva by the hand into the palace. Shatrughna has already prepared it with beds, rich hangings and lit lamps.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-13.plain: Bharat asks Sugriva to send fast messengers to gather the holy things needed to crown the king. Sugriva gives four golden jars to four of his swiftest monkeys to fill with water from the four distant seas.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-14.plain: The monkey messengers fly east, west, south and north to the oceans and bring back water. Water from five hundred rivers is also collected for the king.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-15.plain: Vasishtha, the eldest royal priest, seats Rama and Sita on a jeweled throne. He and other great sages pour the pure, holy water on Rama's head.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-16.plain: Priests, young women and warriors all come forward to sprinkle holy water on their king. Even the gods in the sky pour rare herbal juices on his forehead.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-17.plain: Rama is crowned with the ancient gold crown first worn by Manu, the first king of his family line. Shatrughna holds the royal umbrella, and the kings Rama had helped wave fans around him.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-18.plain: The Wind God gives Rama a jeweled gold chain, and Indra, king of the gods, gives him a string of pearls. The skies ring with cheers as heavenly dancers dance and musicians sing.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-19.plain: On that blessed day the fields fill with golden grain, the trees bend with beautiful fruit, and flowers smell sweeter.

ramayana-homecoming-6-130-20.plain: King Rama gives generous gifts to the priests: cows, horses, clothes and jewels. He puts a dazzling jeweled chain on his friend Sugriva and gives bright armlets to Angad, son of Bali.

ramayana-deer-3-44-3.plain: The golden deer keeps teasing Rama. It shows itself clearly, then disappears into the woods, then flashes into view again between the trees like the moon peeking out from clouds.
themes: the chase of the golden deer

ramayana-deer-3-44-4.plain: The deer is really the demon Maricha in disguise. He keeps appearing and vanishing so that Rama follows him far from his hut. Rama grows angry, upset and tired, and he rests in the shade.
themes: the chase of the golden deer

ramayana-deer-3-44-5.plain: Maricha, the night-roaming demon, shows himself again, walking slowly among other deer close to Rama. This makes Rama angry. Rama goes after him, but the deer suddenly takes fright and runs out of sight again.
themes: the chase of the golden deer

ramayana-deer-3-44-6.plain: Rama leaves the shade and follows the deer once more. Now he is more determined to kill it. Growing impatient, he pulls out a shining, deadly arrow.

ramayana-deer-3-44-7.plain: Rama carefully aims and shoots an arrow made by the god Brahma. It flies like a fiery snake or a lightning bolt of Indra, the king of the gods, and strikes the false deer in the heart.

ramayana-deer-3-44-8.plain: Maricha leaps once and falls, dying, with a terrible roar. As he dies he drops the deer form. Still loyal to his master Ravana, he plans how to make Sita send her protector Lakshmana away so Ravana can capture her.

ramayana-deer-3-44-9.plain: Knowing the moment has come, Maricha shouts "Ho, Sita! Lakshmana!" in a voice that sounds exactly like Rama's.

ramayana-deer-3-44-10.plain: Struck by the arrow, Maricha leaves the deer shape, returns to his giant demon form and dies. Seeing him bleeding, Rama thinks of Sita at once. He remembers Lakshmana's warning that the deer was Maricha's trick.

ramayana-deer-3-44-11.plain: Rama realizes the creature was Maricha. He worries that if Sita heard the demon's cry in his own voice, she must be terribly frightened.
themes: anxiety about what is happening at home

ramayana-deer-3-44-12.plain: Rama wonders what Lakshmana must think after hearing the cry. His hair stands on end, and dread fills his heart as he thinks of the dead demon and that cry.

ramayana-deer-3-44-13.plain: Rama hunts and kills another deer, carries it with him, and hurries back toward his home in the Janasthan forest.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-1.plain: After Sita is taken, Lakshmana comforts Rama with wise advice. Rama listens, controls his strong grief and anger, and, leaning on his bow, asks Lakshmana where they should search next and how to find her.
themes: what to do next after a loss

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-2.plain: Lakshmana answers his tired, grieving brother: even if their search has failed so far, they should search the dangerous Janasthan forest again.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-3.plain: Lakshmana describes the land: deep caves, cliffs and dark pits, home to animals and to heavenly beings like Gandharvas (celestial musicians) and Kinnaras (forest spirits).

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-4.plain: Lakshmana says they should search every hill and cave together. He tells Rama that great people like him, wise and sharp-sighted, do not give up in hard times, but stand firm like mountains in a storm.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-5.plain: Angry, Rama readies an arrow and searches the forest with Lakshmana. They find Jatayu, the great vulture, lying bloody on the ground, as huge as a broken mountain peak. Rama looks at him in rage.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-6.plain: Rama wrongly decides that the vulture is a demon in disguise who has eaten Sita. He vows to shoot it.

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-7.plain: Rama rushes at the bird with his arrow ready, his steps shaking the earth. The dying Jatayu, with blood on his beak, tries to speak to Rama, son of King Dasharatha.
themes: a friend mistaken for an enemy

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-8.plain: Jatayu tells Rama that the lady he is searching for has been taken by the fierce demon king Ravana, who has also given Jatayu his fatal wound. It happened when Rama and Lakshmana had both left Sita unprotected.
themes: bad news about a loved one

ramayana-jatayu-3-68-9.plain: Jatayu says he saw Ravana carrying Sita away and rushed to help her. He smashed Ravana's chariot and royal umbrella and knocked Ravana to the ground.

ramayana-exile-2-40-18.plain: Sumantra, the royal charioteer, has to ignore the people begging him to stop and drives Rama away. So many people cry along the road that their tears settle the dust kicked up by the chariot wheels.

ramayana-exile-2-40-19.plain: The women weep, their tears falling like water splashed from lotus flowers by darting fish. King Dasharatha sees that the whole town shares one sorrow, and he collapses like a tall tree cut at the root.

ramayana-exile-2-40-20.plain: The crowd following Rama's chariot sees the king faint and cries out loudly. They shout Rama's name and grieve for his mother, weeping around the sorrowing queens.

ramayana-exile-2-40-21.plain: Rama looks back and sees his father lying weak and confused, and his mother running after him. Held by his duty to go, he cannot bear to look into his mother's eyes, like a trapped young animal that cannot face its mother.

ramayana-exile-2-40-22.plain: Rama sees his parents, who should be riding in comfort, walking wearily after him. Their despair hurts him like a goad hurts an elephant, so he tells Sumantra to drive on fast.

ramayana-exile-2-40-23.plain: Rama's mother Kausalya runs toward the chariot like a cow rushing to her calf. Rama keeps looking back at her as she cries out wildly for Sita, Lakshmana and her son.

ramayana-exile-2-40-24.plain: The king shouts for the chariot to stop, while Rama shouts for it to go on. Sumantra is torn between the two. Rama says a long, drawn-out sorrow is the worst pain.

ramayana-exile-2-40-25.plain: Rama tells Sumantra to keep going, and if the king is angry, to say he did not hear him. Sumantra obeys, sends the crowd back, and drives the horses at full speed.

ramayana-exile-2-40-26.plain: The king's attendants turn back after honoring Rama, but in their hearts they stay with him. The king's ministers tell Dasharatha that following someone you hope to see return is useless.

ramayana-exile-2-40-27.plain: Weak and downcast, the king listens to their wise advice. Still, he and the queen keep watching their son for as long as they can.

ramayana-deer-3-43-1.plain: While picking flowers, Sita keeps staring at an amazing deer with a back and sides shining in silver and gold.

ramayana-deer-3-43-2.plain: Sita excitedly calls out again and again to Rama and his brother Lakshmana to come quickly and see the wonderful deer.

ramayana-deer-3-43-3.plain: The brothers rush to Sita and see the deer. But Lakshmana feels strong doubt and speaks up about his fear.

ramayana-deer-3-43-4.plain: Lakshmana warns that the deer may be the demon Maricha in disguise. He says kings who came hunting here before were tricked and killed by such tricks.

ramayana-deer-3-43-5.plain: Lakshmana says Maricha is skilled in magic and takes the shape of a deer. No real deer has ever shone with gold and jewels like this, so it must be magic.

ramayana-deer-3-43-6.plain: Sita, already caught by the demon's trick, brushes aside Lakshmana's careful warning. She tells Rama the deer's rare beauty delights her.

ramayana-deer-3-43-7.plain: Sita asks Rama to go and bring her the deer. She says many animals—cows, deer, monkeys, bears and Kinnaras (half-human forest beings)—wander near their hermitage without harm.

ramayana-deer-3-43-8.plain: Sita says that none of the animals she has seen ever charmed her like this one. It glows with jewels and lights up the forest like the rising moon.

ramayana-deer-3-43-9.plain: Sita says the deer's beauty is beyond words and has captured her heart. She begs Rama to catch it alive so he too can enjoy looking at it.
themes: asking a loved one for a favor

ramayana-deer-3-43-10.plain: Sita imagines that after their forest exile ends and they return to rule, the deer will decorate her home. She says it will delight Bharata, the queens and herself.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-5.plain: Shatrughna, Rama's youngest brother, keeps giving orders. Workers should sprinkle cool water on the road and scatter flowers along Rama's path. Banners should fly from towers and temples, and the roofs should be covered with flowers.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-6.plain: The nobles hurry to carry out Shatrughna's orders. They ride out on elephants wearing jewelled straps, with thousands of people around them carrying flags.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-7.plain: A thousand chiefs ride horses and a thousand more ride shining chariots, while huge crowds follow on foot. The widowed queens of the late King Dasharatha travel in curtained litters, chairs carried on poles.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-8.plain: Kausalya, Rama's mother and the senior queen, leads the women, and Sumitra and the other ladies follow her. Then Bharat joins the crowd full of joy. Brahmans (priests) in white robes surround him, singing, while people cheer and drums, conch shells and tambours sound.
themes: a mother waiting for her son

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-9.plain: Bharat still carries Rama's sandals on his head as a sign of respect, because he ruled only in Rama's name. A white royal umbrella and golden fans are ready for Rama. But as they come near the town of Nandigrama, there is still no sign of Rama.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-10.plain: Worried and sad, Bharat asks Hanuman, the monkey chief, whether he has played a trick on him, as monkeys are said to do. He asks where Rama is, because he cannot see the shape-shifting monkey army anywhere.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-11.plain: Hanuman, son of the Wind God, answers Bharat's eager question. He points to trees full of fruit and buzzing with bees. A holy sage has made them bear fruit out of season to honour Rama.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-12.plain: Hanuman says this power comes from an old blessing given by Indra, king of the gods. He tells Bharat to listen to the shouts of the monkeys. They are about to cross the Gomati river.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-13.plain: Hanuman sees the flying chariot coming. The god Brahma designed it, and it shines like the moon and flies wherever its rider wishes. It once belonged to Ravana, the demon king, and Rama won it when Ravana died.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-14.plain: Hanuman points them out. Rama and Lakshmana stand in the chariot with Sita, the rescued queen, between them. With them are Vibhishana, Ravana's good brother, and Sugriva, the monkey king, with his followers.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-15.plain: Everyone, young and old, men and women, shouts together, "It's Rama!" They all jump down from their elephants, chariots and horses. Every eye is fixed on Rama's shining face.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-16.plain: Bharat stares for a moment, amazed. Then he folds his hands in respect and greets his brother. He climbs into the chariot and bows at Rama's feet, and Rama lifts him up and hugs him tightly.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-17.plain: Bharat greets Lakshmana and Sita, saying his own name to each of them. Then he greets Sugriva, the monkey king, along with Jambavan, Angada (Bali's son) and every other chief, leaving no one out.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-18.plain: Bharat hugs Sugriva and thanks him. He says there were four brothers, and now Sugriva is the fifth. He adds that you know a friend by their kind actions, and you know an enemy by the harm they do.
themes: how to know a true friend

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-19.plain: Bharat thanks Vibhishana for fighting bravely for Rama. Shatrughna also shows his love and respect to both of his older brothers and bows at Sita's feet.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-20.plain: Rama goes to his mother Kausalya and sees how pale and thin her grief has made her. He comforts her gently and holds her feet with love. He also bows to Sumitra and to Kaikeyi, whose wish had sent him into exile, and he greets every lady and the family priest.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-21.plain: A huge crowd shouts, "Welcome, Rama, whom we missed so long!" Bharat puts Rama's sandals back on his feet. He says he is returning the kingdom that he looked after in Rama's place through years of pain.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-22.plain: Bharat says he no longer grieves over his past sorrows. His life feels blessed now that he sees Rama come home to rule.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-23.plain: Everyone admires Bharat's faithful love, and even the monkey chiefs cry tender tears. Rama hugs his brother again. Then he goes to the grove where Bharat had lived simply, like a hermit, while he waited.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-24.plain: Rama gets down in that holy place and walks happily on the ground. Then at his command the flying chariot rises and flies north, back to Kubera, the Lord of Wealth, who first owned it.

ramayana-exile-2-19-21.plain: Rama has just lost his chance to be king, yet his face still shines like the autumn moon. He greets the crowd kindly in his gentle voice and walks to his mother's house.

ramayana-exile-2-19-22.plain: His brother Lakshmana follows him, deeply upset but hiding it. Rama enters the palace, where everyone is happy and hopeful, knowing his news will destroy their joy.

ramayana-exile-2-19-23.plain: Rama does not let himself break down. He keeps the terrible news to himself for now so that his loyal friends are not hurt by it yet.

ramayana-exile-2-40-1.plain: Rama, his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana bow at King Dasaratha's feet and walk around him in respect. With the king's permission to leave, Rama and Sita honor the heartbroken queen.

ramayana-exile-2-40-2.plain: Lakshmana lovingly bows at the feet of his mother, Sumitra. She tells him to take faithful care of Rama in the forest.

ramayana-exile-2-40-3.plain: Sumitra tells Lakshmana that Rama is his protector in good times and bad. She says the younger brothers of their family always serve the eldest, give generously, and fight bravely.
themes: standing by someone in hard times

ramayana-exile-2-40-4.plain: Sumitra tells Lakshmana to treat Rama as his father, Sita as his mother, and their forest hut as his home city of Ayodhya. Then she blesses him and sends him off.
themes: home is where your loved ones are

ramayana-exile-2-40-5.plain: Sumitra wishes her son success, victory over enemies, and happiness, and hopes he comes home joyfully at the end.
themes: hoping a loved one returns safely

ramayana-exile-2-40-6.plain: Sumantra, the royal charioteer, joins his palms in respect and invites Rama to climb into the chariot. He promises to drive him swiftly wherever he wants to go.

ramayana-exile-2-40-7.plain: Sumantra says Rama's fourteen years of exile in the forest must start today, because Queen Kaikeyi, who demanded the exile, is insisting he leave.

ramayana-exile-2-40-8.plain: Once she is ready, Sita calmly climbs into the shining chariot. Rama and Lakshmana jump in after her.
themes: calm in the face of change

ramayana-exile-2-40-9.plain: The king had given Sita clothes and jewels to last the years away. The brothers pack hunting nets, weapons, armor, a leather basket and a spade into the chariot.

ramayana-exile-2-40-10.plain: Sumantra drives the fast horses forward. As Rama leaves for exile, the whole city of Ayodhya is overcome with grief, and even the horses and elephants cry out.

ramayana-exile-2-40-11.plain: People of every age rush to the chariot and cling to it, weeping. They beg Sumantra to slow down.

ramayana-exile-2-40-12.plain: The people want one last look at Rama before he is gone for years. They say his mother must have a heart of iron to watch him go and survive it.

ramayana-exile-2-40-13.plain: The crowd praises Sita, princess of Videha, for staying by Rama like his shadow. They praise Lakshmana too for faithfully serving his godlike, kind-spoken brother.

ramayana-exile-2-40-14.plain: The people tell Lakshmana his firm loyalty will bring him success and lead him to heaven with Rama. Crying, they keep following the chariot of their beloved prince.

ramayana-exile-2-40-15.plain: King Dasaratha, surrounded by his sad wives, hurries out crying that he must see his dear son once more. The women weep as he comes near.

ramayana-exile-2-40-16.plain: The queens cry like female elephants whose leader has died. The great king looks troubled, like the full moon darkened by an eclipse.

ramayana-exile-2-40-17.plain: Rama tells the charioteer to go faster and not linger, while the people cry out for him to stay.
themes: leaving when others beg you to stay

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-13.plain: Sugriva, the exiled monkey king, asks Rama to free him from his suffering and fear. He says that rescuing a friend in trouble is a noble task, worthy of a hero like Rama.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-14.plain: Rama, who knows what is right and has no trickery in him, smiles gently and answers Sugriva. He says that friends who trust him and ask for his help are never let down.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-15.plain: Rama promises to kill Bali, Sugriva's brother, who stole Sugriva's wife. He describes his arrows as bright as the sun, as strong as Indra's thunderbolt (Indra is the king of the gods), and as deadly as angry snakes.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-16.plain: Rama tells Sugriva that this very day he will see his longtime enemy lying dead like a broken mountain, struck down by Rama's bow.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-17.plain: Sugriva is filled with joy at Rama's words. He thanks Rama, saying that with his help he will get back his kingdom and his beloved wife.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-18.plain: Sugriva asks Rama to stop his older brother Bali so he can never again take away Sugriva's rights or hurt him. The friendship pact is made, and it will bring joy to Sita and the monkey king but sorrow to the demons.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-19.plain: At that moment Sita's left eye twitches, which for a woman was a lucky sign, and she feels hope. But Bali's left eye also twitches, a bad sign for a man, warning of his death that day.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-20.plain: The demons also feel their left eyes twitch, and they know it is a sign that trouble is coming for them.

ramayana-leap-5-1-1.plain: Hanuman, the monkey hero, decides to fly through the sky to find where Sita, Rama's captured wife, is being held by Ravan, the demon king. He stands ready and strong, like a mighty bull, for this brave task.
themes: getting ready for a big challenge

ramayana-leap-5-1-2.plain: Hanuman walks like a lion over the shining grass. His heavy steps scare the animals into hiding, crush trees, and frighten the birds.

ramayana-leap-5-1-3.plain: The mountain where Hanuman stands is beautiful, with lilies of many colors and rocks shining with metals. Heavenly beings like Gandharvas (heavenly musicians), Yakshas (nature spirits), and serpent gods wander there.

ramayana-leap-5-1-4.plain: Hanuman happily roams the wooded mountain top, like a shining snake playing in a lake. Then he stops to pray to the saints and gods.

ramayana-leap-5-1-5.plain: Hanuman prays to Svayambhu (Brahma, the creator), the Sun, the Wind, and Indra for help. Then he tells the other monkeys he will fly to Ravan's city like an arrow from Rama's bow, and if he can't find Sita there, he'll search the sky or even heaven, or bring Ravan back tied up.

ramayana-leap-5-1-6.plain: Hanuman gathers his strength and jumps from the mountain. Trees are pulled up and follow after him, his huge shadow races across the ocean like a ship, and the sea swells beneath him.

ramayana-leap-5-1-7.plain: The gods shower flowers on Hanuman, heavenly singers cheer, and saints praise him. The Sea itself wants to help him and serve Rama.

ramayana-leap-5-1-8.plain: The Sea, wanting to help for Rama's sake, speaks to the mountain Mainaka. It reminds Mainaka that long ago the gods gave it the job of keeping the Asuras (demon enemies of the gods) trapped deep below.

ramayana-leap-5-1-9.plain: The Sea continues: Mainaka guards the cursed demons so they cannot escape, standing at the gates of the underworld. It also has the power to grow or rise up out of the water.

ramayana-leap-5-1-10.plain: The Sea asks Mainaka to rise up out of the water. Hanuman is flying overhead on a great mission for Rama, and the Sea wants Mainaka to give him a place to rest on his tiring journey.
themes: helping someone on a hard journey

ramayana-leap-5-1-11.plain: Mainaka hears the Sea and rises quickly out of the water, covered in plants and trees. Its golden peaks shine as bright as a hundred suns above the waves.

ramayana-leap-5-1-12.plain: Hanuman thinks the rising mountain is trying to block his way, so he knocks it down as he flies. But from the falling mountain comes a friendly voice calling out to him.
themes: misjudging a friend as an enemy

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-13.plain: Hanuman, who is very skilled with words, finishes speaking. Rama (called the son of Raghu, his ancestor) is delighted by the messenger's speech and turns happily to his brother Lakshman to speak.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-14.plain: Rama tells Lakshman that this is the advisor of Sugriva, the good monkey king (Vanar means monkey-folk) Rama has wanted to meet. He asks Lakshman to reply kindly to this eloquent messenger.
themes: meeting someone you hoped to meet

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-15.plain: Rama says that anyone who speaks this beautifully must know the holy Vedas well, the Rig, Yajur and Sama Vedas, and must have studied grammar carefully.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-16.plain: Rama notes that Hanuman spoke a long speech without a single mistake. Nothing in his eyes, face or body showed any lie or trickery.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-17.plain: Rama praises how Hanuman spoke: short, steady, sweet and clear, with no hurtful words. His voice was calm and even, neither rushed nor halting, and it won the heart.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-18.plain: Rama says Hanuman's clear, well-formed speech could calm even an enemy about to strike. A ruler without such a messenger would struggle to succeed.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-19.plain: Rama says no leader's plans can fail when he is helped by someone this wise and well-spoken.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-20.plain: Lakshman, also a skilled speaker, answers Hanuman. He says they already know of Sugriva's good qualities, came here to meet him, and will gladly do what Sugriva asks.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-3-21.plain: Hanuman is overjoyed by Lakshman's wise reply. He hopes this friendship will help his king Sugriva win back what he lost.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-1.plain: Hanuman goes from Rishyamuka hill to Malaya hill and tells his king Sugriva that Rama, famous in many lands, has come with Lakshman.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-2.plain: Hanuman describes Rama: he is brave even against a thousand enemies, the son of King Dasharatha, the pride of the Ikshvaku family, and he still follows his duty by obeying his father.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-3.plain: Hanuman adds that Rama's father performed great sacred fire rituals, gave away a huge number of cows, rewarded the priests, and ruled well, famous for truthfulness and self-control.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-5.plain: Sugriva listens to Hanuman with joy and tells Rama that Hanuman has truly described his good qualities: his training in duty and his real care for everyone.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-6.plain: Sugriva says the greatest honor of his life would be for Rama to become his friend. He offers his hand as a promise of friendship that will never be broken.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-7.plain: Rama joyfully takes Sugriva's hand and hugs him as a friend. Hanuman drops his beggar disguise and shows his real form.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-8.plain: Hanuman rubs pieces of wood together to start a fire and decorates it with flowers. Rama and Sugriva respectfully walk around the fire together to seal their friendship.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-9.plain: Bound by their promise, the two friends gaze at each other happily. Sugriva tells Rama that he is his dearest friend and they will share each other's joys and troubles.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-10.plain: Sugriva breaks a flowering branch of a Sal tree to make a seat for himself and Rama. Hanuman gives Lakshman a branch of sandalwood to sit on.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-11.plain: Still trembling with joy, Sugriva tells Rama that he is full of sorrow and fear, rejected by his enemies and wandering in exile.

ramayana-hanuman-meets-rama-4-5-12.plain: Sugriva explains that he has lost his wife and lives alone in the forest, sometimes fleeing in terror. His brother Bali has wronged and troubled him for a long time.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-13.plain: Rama looks at the dead vulture Jatayu, huge as a hill, and in deep sorrow speaks to his brother Lakshmana. He says this bird lived happily in this wild forest for many years.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-14.plain: Rama says Jatayu lived for many peaceful years in the Dandaka forest, a place full of demons, and now he has died there. No one can escape what fate decides.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-15.plain: Rama tells Lakshmana that Jatayu died fighting bravely for him, trying to rescue Sita from the demon Ravana. The king of the vultures gave up his life for Rama's sake, even though he lost the fight.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-16.plain: Rama says that even among animals we often find great, good souls who follow what is right and protect the weak. He says that seeing this bird dead hurts him even more than losing Sita.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-17.plain: Rama says Jatayu was as honored and loved as his own father, King Dasharatha. He asks Lakshmana to bring wood, because he will light the funeral fire himself and lay the bird on it.
themes: gratitude to those who helped us

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-18.plain: Rama says he will burn the body of the king of birds with full honor. He prays that Jatayu, the noble-hearted bird, will go to heaven as a reward for his faithful love.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-19.plain: Rama blesses Jatayu to live happily in heaven among those who worshipped faithfully, the brave who never gave up, and the generous who gave land to others.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-20.plain: With a heavy heart, Rama lays Jatayu on the funeral pyre and lights the fire to burn his friend's body. Then Rama and Lakshmana go on into the forest.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-23.plain: Jatayu, after his brave deed and honored by Rama, rises to heaven. After finishing all the funeral rites, the brothers feel some comfort and leave the river.

ramayana-jatayu-3-69-24.plain: The two brothers, looking like gods, walk on through the forest. Each of them thinks about how to find the one who kidnapped Sita.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-1.plain: Following the advice of Kabandha, a demon Rama had freed, the princes travel east through the forest toward Lake Pampa. On the way, trees full of honey-sweet fruit delight them.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-2.plain: Tired, the brothers rest for the night on a forested mountain. At dawn they reach the west side of Lake Pampa and see the lovely, quiet home of Shabari, a holy woman living in the forest.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-3.plain: The princes reach Shabari's holy grove, full of beautiful trees. The old, devoted woman comes to meet them with joined hands, bows low, and touches their feet in welcome.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-4.plain: Shabari gives them water to drink and to wash their feet, as a good host should. Rama then speaks to this pure woman who never broke a rule of right living.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-5.plain: Rama kindly asks Shabari if she is at peace, if her spiritual practice is growing, and if she has conquered anger while living on little food. He asks if she keeps her vows, has peace of mind, and has been rewarded for serving her teachers.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-6.plain: Shabari, pure and honored by all the sages, stands beside Rama and gently answers. She says that meeting him today is the full reward of all her years of spiritual effort.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-7.plain: Shabari says that today her life has found its purpose and her service to the sages was not wasted. By honoring Rama, whom she sees as divine, she has earned heaven.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-8.plain: Shabari tells Rama that his kind look makes her soul pure and that through his grace she will find bliss. She says her teachers, the sages, went up to heaven in shining chariots back when Rama was living at Chitrakuta mountain.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-9.plain: Shabari says that as her teachers rose to heaven, they told her that Rama and Lakshmana would soon visit her grove. They told her to honor them well as guests.

ramayana-shabari-3-75-10.plain: Shabari says the sages promised that after seeing Rama she would go to heavenly worlds that never end. She tells Rama she has gathered a big store of all kinds of forest fruit for him from around Lake Pampa.

ramayana-leap-5-1-33.plain: As Hanuman flies over the sea, a cruel demoness named Sinhika spots him. She can change her shape. She grabs his shadow, happy that she will finally eat.

ramayana-leap-5-1-34.plain: Hanuman feels himself held back, like a ship that cannot move against the wind. He looks below and above to find out what is stopping him.

ramayana-leap-5-1-35.plain: Hanuman sees the ugly monster rise out of the sea. He remembers that King Sugriva had warned him about a demon who catches creatures by grabbing their shadows.

ramayana-leap-5-1-36.plain: Hanuman makes his body grow huge, like a rain cloud. The demoness opens her jaws enormously wide and rushes at him with a roar to eat him.

ramayana-leap-5-1-37.plain: Quick as a thought, Hanuman shrinks his body and jumps right inside her open mouth. He disappears into it, like the moon swallowed by Rahu, the demon said to cause eclipses.

ramayana-leap-5-1-39.plain: The heavenly spirits watch the demoness die and cheer for Hanuman. They tell him to go on with his good mission, saying someone with his courage, wisdom and skill cannot fail.

ramayana-leap-5-1-40.plain: Happy with their praise, Hanuman flies on and nearly reaches the far shore. He sees a dark line of forest and the green island of Lanka, full of flowers, trees and streams.
themes: the end of a long journey

ramayana-leap-5-1-41.plain: Hanuman lands on a mountain peak called Lamba, streaked with colored minerals. From there he looks at the beautiful city of Lanka shining on the mountain like a crown.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-1.plain: The god of the Ocean speaks to Rama, the son of the Raghu family. He says that Nala, a monkey who is the son of Vishvakarma, the builder of the gods, has inherited some of his father's heavenly building skill.
themes: finding the right person for the job

ramayana-bridge-6-22-2.plain: The Ocean tells Rama to call Nala, who has divine skill, to build a bridge across the sea.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-3.plain: The Ocean disappears. Nala, a great monkey leader, tells Rama he will build a bridge over the dangerous sea, because he shares his father's skill and has the power and the will.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-4.plain: Nala says that gentle methods do not work on an ungrateful heart. The Ocean only gave way because Rama threatened him, so only fear made it let them pass.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-5.plain: Nala explains that before he was born, Vishvakarma promised his mother Mandari her son would be almost as skilled as him. Then Nala stops praising himself and asks Rama to order the monkeys to start building the bridge today.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-6.plain: At Rama's command, the monkey army jumps up and goes into the forest. They pull up trees and drag the wood to the sea.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-7.plain: The monkeys bend and pull down all kinds of trees, such as palms, ashokas, sal trees and bamboos, along with flowering vines.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-8.plain: Using machines, the monkeys topple rocks and whole hills. Water shoots into the air and falls like rain, and the ocean roars and heaves as the mountains fall in.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-9.plain: The monkeys build a very strong bridge a hundred leagues long. They tie huge rocks with ropes and throw them in, along with broken pieces of hills and trees still in flower.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-10.plain: The work is loud and wild as giant rocks crash into the sea. On the first day they build fourteen leagues, twenty more on the second, and by sunset on the fifth day the whole bridge is finished.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-11.plain: The monkeys rush across the bridge, and it does not shake under their countless steps. Vibhishana, Ravana's brother who joined Rama, stands on the shore holding his mace, impatient to move on.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-12.plain: King Sugriva tells Rama to climb on Hanuman's broad back, and says Angad will carry Lakshmana. The two monkeys will carry them through the air above the sea.

ramayana-leap-5-1-13.plain: The mountain rises again to meet Hanuman as he flies. Standing on its top peak in human form, the mountain spirit greets him and says his task is a great one.
themes: a helper appears on the way
respect for someone on a mission

ramayana-leap-5-1-14.plain: The mountain asks Hanuman to land and rest for a while. It explains that the Sea owes a debt to Rama's family, the line of Raghu, so the Sea wants to honour Rama's messenger.

ramayana-leap-5-1-15.plain: The mountain says the Sea told it to rise up from the water so Hanuman could rest on its peak. It invites him to rest his tired body and eat its sweet fruit.

ramayana-leap-5-1-16.plain: The mountain says it knows Hanuman's fame, which all three worlds talk about, and that no one leaps through the sky like him. Wise people honour every guest, even a humble one, so it cannot ignore such a great guest.

ramayana-leap-5-1-17.plain: The mountain says Hanuman shares the strength of his father, the Wind God, and honouring the son also honours the father. Then it begins a story: long ago, in the first age, mountains had wings and flew wherever they liked.

ramayana-leap-5-1-18.plain: The gods and sages were afraid the flying mountains would fall on them. So Indra, king of the gods, cut off their wings with his thunderbolts, but the Wind God saved this mountain by hiding it under the ocean.

ramayana-leap-5-1-19.plain: Because the Wind God saved it, the mountain still has its wings. To thank him, it wants to honour his son Hanuman, and it asks him again to rest.

ramayana-leap-5-1-20.plain: Hanuman says he cannot stop or turn aside from his task. But he is pleased and accepts the mountain's kind wish as if he had received the gift.

ramayana-leap-5-1-21.plain: Hanuman lightly touches the mountain's peak with his hand, then leaps high into the sky, happy in his strength. He flies on through the blue sky, the path of his father the Wind.

ramayana-leap-5-1-22.plain: The gods and sages watch this amazing flight. They go to Surasa, mother of the Nagas (serpent beings), and ask her to block Hanuman's way.

ramayana-leap-5-1-23.plain: The gods tell Surasa to take the form of a huge, frightening demon with red eyes and tusks. They want to test Hanuman's strength and see whether he will escape by cleverness or be beaten.

ramayana-leap-5-1-24.plain: Surasa agrees and rises from the sea in a terrifying shape. She roars at Hanuman that he is meant to be her food today, by a gift granted to her long ago by Brahma, the creator god.

ramayana-leap-5-1-25.plain: Hanuman is not frightened. He explains that Rama and his wife Sita were living in the Dandak forest when Ravan, king of the demons, stole Sita away.

ramayana-leap-5-1-26.plain: Hanuman says he is going to Sita as Rama's willing messenger and should not be stopped. He promises on his honour that after he finds Sita and reports to Rama, he will come back and let her eat him.

ramayana-leap-5-1-27.plain: Surasa refuses his offer. She says Brahma's gift means he must enter her mouth, and only then may he go on.

ramayana-leap-5-1-28.plain: Angry, Hanuman dares her to open her jaws wider and grows ten leagues tall. Her mouth opens to twenty leagues wide.

ramayana-leap-5-1-29.plain: Hanuman grows to fifty leagues, but her mouth keeps growing too. Then he suddenly shrinks smaller than a thumb, darts into her mouth, and jumps right back out.

ramayana-leap-5-1-30.plain: Hanging in the air, Hanuman smiles and says goodbye to Surasa, daughter of Daksha. He has entered her mouth, so her gift from Brahma is fulfilled, and now he goes to find Sita.

ramayana-leap-5-1-31.plain: Surasa returns to her true form and blesses Hanuman. She wishes him success and hopes he brings Sita back to Rama in triumph.

ramayana-leap-5-1-32.plain: Spirits watching praise Hanuman's courage. He flies fast as Garud, king of birds, through the clouds where heavenly musicians live, past the rainbow and the shining chariots of the gods.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-13.plain: Rama and Lakshmana, the princes of the Ikshvaku family, ride across on the backs of Hanuman and Angad, leading the army with King Sugriva. Behind them the huge monkey army (the Vanars) follows, some running over the water and some flying through the air.

ramayana-bridge-6-22-14.plain: The army is so loud that it drowns out the roar of the ocean as they rush over the bridge that Nala designed. They reach the shore of Lanka and rest by streams under trees full of fruit.

ramayana-ravana-6-110-1.plain: Matali, the driver of the chariot sent by the gods, tells Rama to stop wasting effort with ordinary weapons against Ravana. He urges Rama to use the special arrow made by Brahma, the Creator.
themes: good advice in a hard fight

ramayana-ravana-6-110-2.plain: Rama, the son of the Raghu family, follows the advice and fits a hissing, never-missing arrow to his bow. It was given to him by the sage Agastya, and Brahma had first made it to help Indra, king of the gods.

ramayana-ravana-6-110-3.plain: The arrow is described as made of great powers: the wind gave it feathers, the sun and fire gave its point its blaze, and the great mountains Meru and Mandara gave it weight.

ramayana-ravana-6-110-4.plain: Rama aims the arrow at Ravana, the lord of Lanka, and it pierces his chest and heart. Ravana falls dead, like the demon Vritra killed by Indra's thunderbolt.
themes: the end of a long struggle

ramayana-ravana-6-110-5.plain: When Ravana falls, his Rakshasa (demon) army screams, gives up hope, and runs back through Lanka's gates. The monkey army shouts with joy and praises the victorious Rama.
themes: losing hope when the leader falls

ramayana-ravana-6-110-6.plain: Heavenly musicians play, a cool sweet breeze blows, and flowers rain down from the sky. Voices praise Rama as the champion of the gods, saying 'well done.'

ramayana-ravana-6-111-1.plain: Vibhishana, Ravana's brother who had joined Rama's side, sees Ravana dead and cannot hold back his sorrow. He bends over the body and cries out, calling his brother brave and skilled in war.

ramayana-ravana-6-111-2.plain: Vibhishana asks why his brother lies on the cold, bloody ground instead of a soft bed. He says he had warned Ravana this would happen, but Ravana's pride would not let him listen to a friend's criticism.
themes: regret over a family member's choices

ramayana-ravana-6-111-3.plain: Vibhishana says their sun and moon, the light of their people, has gone out. All of Ravana's brightness could not stand against Rama's arrows.

ramayana-ravana-6-111-4.plain: Vibhishana compares Ravana to a tall, beautiful royal tree whose flowers were his good deeds and his sons. Now the tree lies broken on the ground.
themes: the fall of a great family

ramayana-ravana-6-111-5.plain: Rama tells Vibhishana not to grieve, because Ravana died bravely in battle, the way a warrior should. He asks him to stay strong and carry out the duties that are left.

ramayana-ravana-6-111-6.plain: Vibhishana says Ravana had once defeated the gods and Indra and was never beaten before. He threw himself at Rama and was broken, like ocean waves smashing against a rock.

ramayana-ravana-6-111-7.plain: Vibhishana mourns Ravana as a generous lord, a loyal friend, and a protector of his people. He asks Rama to let Ravana receive proper funeral honors.

ramayana-ravana-6-111-8.plain: Rama answers that hatred ends when the enemy is dead, and now the victory brings peace between them. He tells Vibhishana to hold the funeral properly and offers to help.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-1.plain: Bharat, Rama's brother who had ruled while Rama was away, is overjoyed to hear that Rama is coming home. He tells his brother Shatrughna to decorate every temple with flowers, burn incense, and play music.
themes: joy at a loved one's return

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-2.plain: Bharat orders everyone to go out to meet their king with drums, singers, and poets who know the old stories. He also calls for the royal ladies and the nobles of the council.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-3.plain: Bharat asks that all the most loved and honored people, the priests (Brahmans) and the soldiers, go together to bring the king home in triumph.

ramayana-homecoming-6-129-4.plain: Shatrughna happily obeys his brother. He orders ten thousand men to work hard and smooth the road for Rama, the king of Koshala.

ramayana-exile-2-19-1.plain: Queen Kaikeyi has just told Rama he must go into exile. Rama, the prince who defeats his enemies, stays calm and is not shaken by her cruel words.

ramayana-exile-2-19-2.plain: Rama agrees to go and live alone in the forest, dressed like a hermit with matted hair, so that his father's promise is kept. He only wants to know why the king seems so harsh today.

ramayana-exile-2-19-3.plain: Rama asks why his father, the king, will not greet him warmly as before. He tells Kaikeyi not to be angry, because he truly means it: he will go to the forest as a hermit.
themes: hurt by a loved one's distance

ramayana-exile-2-19-4.plain: Rama says he could never refuse his father, who is his friend, master and king. His only pain is that his father did not tell him himself that he wanted Bharata, Rama's brother, to be king.
themes: hurt that a parent didn't tell you directly

ramayana-exile-2-19-5.plain: Rama says he would gladly give Bharata everything, even his wife, kingdom, wealth and life, without being asked. He would give it even more gladly if it saves his father's honor and makes Kaikeyi happy.
themes: letting go of what you want

ramayana-exile-2-19-6.plain: Rama asks Kaikeyi to free the king from his shame and give him peace. He also asks why the king lies on the floor looking down, with tears running down his face.
themes: shame and guilt in the family

ramayana-exile-2-19-7.plain: Rama tells Kaikeyi to send fast riders to her father's home to bring Bharata back. He will not question his father's words and will leave that very day for the Dandaka forest for fourteen years.

ramayana-exile-2-19-8.plain: Kaikeyi is overjoyed at Rama's answer. Relying on the promise the king made her, she agrees to send the fastest messengers to bring Bharata home.
themes: a promise used as a weapon

ramayana-exile-2-19-9.plain: Kaikeyi pushes Rama to leave for the forest right now. She says that if the ashamed king cannot speak to him, Rama should forgive it and not worry about such a small thing.

ramayana-exile-2-19-10.plain: Kaikeyi says the king will not bathe or eat until Rama has hurried out of the city into the forest.

ramayana-exile-2-19-11.plain: The king cries out in grief and faints on his golden couch, and Rama lifts him up. Kaikeyi shows no pity and keeps urging Rama with bitter words, but Rama listens calmly and answers gently.

ramayana-exile-2-19-12.plain: Rama says he does not want to live as a slave to money or gain. He wants to follow the path of right action like the saints, and would not even run from death to please his father.

ramayana-exile-2-19-13.plain: Rama says that, of all duties, the most important is for a son to obey his father's word. Even without hearing it from the king himself, he will go to the forest for fourteen years if Kaikeyi says so.

ramayana-exile-2-19-14.plain: Rama tells Kaikeyi she must think he has no goodness, since she asked the king for this instead of simply asking Rama himself. He will leave today, but first he will comfort his wife Sita and say goodbye to his mother.

ramayana-exile-2-19-15.plain: Rama tells Kaikeyi it is now her job to make sure Bharata follows his father's command and rules the land fairly, as the eternal law requires.
themes: caring for the kingdom after you leave

ramayana-exile-2-19-16.plain: The king hears everything, weeping loudly but unable to speak. Rama touches the feet of his fainted father and of Kaikeyi, though she did not deserve it, walks around them both in respect, and leaves the room.
themes: a painful farewell to a parent

ramayana-exile-2-19-17.plain: At the gate, Rama finds his close friends waiting. His brother Lakshmana, son of Queen Sumitra, follows him with tearful eyes. Rama sees the vases prepared for his crowning that was supposed to happen that day.

ramayana-exile-2-19-18.plain: Rama respectfully walks around the coronation vases without hanging his head or hurrying. Losing the kingdom does not dull his greatness, just as the moon stays lovely to people even as it shrinks.

ramayana-exile-2-19-19.plain: Accepting exile, Rama gives up his claim to rule and shows no sign of worry. He refuses the royal fans and white umbrella used for kings, and sends away his chariot, servants, friends and townspeople.

ramayana-exile-2-19-20.plain: Rama controls himself and hides the grief inside him as he goes to his mother's house to tell her the sad news. The cheerful people around him cannot see any sign on his face that his fortune has changed.

ramayana-deer-3-43-11.plain: Sita tells Rama that if he cannot catch the golden deer alive, he should shoot it. She dreams of sitting on its soft golden skin spread over the grass.

ramayana-deer-3-43-12.plain: Sita admits that such a strong wish does not suit a gentle lady. But the deer, with its golden hair and sapphire-tipped antlers, has completely charmed her.

ramayana-deer-3-43-13.plain: Sita ends her plea by saying the deer shines like the moon's path or the dawn. She says it has charmed Rama's heart too.

ramayana-deer-3-43-14.plain: Rama listens to Sita, the daughter of King Janak, and looks at the deer again. Charmed by it and wanting to please her, he turns to speak to his brother Lakshman.

ramayana-deer-3-43-15.plain: Rama tells Lakshman to see how badly Sita wants the deer. He says that today it must be killed for its beauty, since it is lovelier than anything in the gardens of the gods, like Nandan.
themes: doing something for someone you love

ramayana-deer-3-43-16.plain: Rama wonders how an earthly forest could hold something so beautiful. He describes its smooth, shining hair and the drops of gold on its side and neck.

ramayana-deer-3-43-17.plain: Rama keeps describing the deer: its red tongue flashes like lightning, its forehead shines with jewel colors, and its neck glows like pearl and shell.

ramayana-deer-3-43-18.plain: Rama says no one could look at such a glowing, jeweled deer without being enchanted and amazed.

ramayana-deer-3-43-19.plain: Rama explains that kings with bows enjoy hunting in the forest. While hunting, they often find treasures too.
themes: the duties and pastimes of kings

ramayana-deer-3-43-20.plain: Rama says a king has the right to treasures he finds in the forest. Such finds feel more precious to him than the riches already in his palace.
themes: value of what we win ourselves

ramayana-deer-3-43-21.plain: Rama notes that careless people often chase gains that turn out empty, as wise people can show. Still, he decides this deer must be hunted so Sita can sit on its golden hide.

ramayana-deer-3-43-22.plain: Rama says he has never seen such a rich, soft coat on any deer, sheep, or goat. He compares the deer to a heavenly star on earth.

ramayana-deer-3-43-23.plain: Rama tells Lakshman that if his fear is right and the deer is really the demon Maricha in disguise, Rama will kill him. Maricha has long terrified the holy hermits of this forest.

ramayana-deer-3-43-25.plain: Rama recalls a demon named Vatapi who tricked holy men by becoming their food and then bursting out of them. When he tried it on the great sage Agastya, Agastya saw through the trick and calmly defeated him.

ramayana-deer-3-43-27.plain: Rama says he will kill Maricha just as Agastya killed his foe. He tells Lakshman to stay armed and guard Sita carefully, following his orders, while he goes to hunt the deer.

ramayana-deer-3-43-28.plain: Rama promises to return with the deer's skin. He points out to Lakshman how much Sita longs for it.
themes: doing something for someone you love

ramayana-deer-3-43-29.plain: Rama tells Lakshman and Sita to stay alert for danger. He expects one arrow to kill the deer so he can bring the skin back quickly.

ramayana-deer-3-43-30.plain: Rama adds that Jatayus, the wise old vulture king and their faithful friend, will help protect Sita. He asks Lakshman to stay watchful, as if enemies were on every side.

ramayana-deer-3-44-1.plain: After warning his brother, Rama takes his golden sword, his beloved bow, and two quivers of arrows, and hurries off.
themes: Rama sets out on the hunt

ramayana-deer-3-44-2.plain: When the deer sees Rama coming, it runs off in fear, then turns to show its head. Rama chases it wherever he glimpses its glowing beauty among the valleys.
